question: The EU is facing a persistent gap in insurance cover in case of natural disasters. According to the Commission, only around 25 % of such damage has been covered by insurance in the past. The 2021 floods in Germany, including in the Ahr valley in Rhineland-Palatinate, and neighbouring countries caused economic damage totalling around EUR 51 billion, of which only around EUR 13 billion were insured.

National budgets often act as insurers of last resort. Between 2022 and 2024, the Commission’s Climate Resilience Dialogue brought together insurers, the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA) and other stakeholders. Its final report proposed measures, including the audit of public-private schemes at EU level.

The Commission has now announced a Climate Insurance Alliance (COM(2026)0720) which is to present a first set of measures by the end of 2027 and to explore possible public-private partnerships at national, regional or EU level. 1.
To what extent will the measures under this Alliance differ from the non-binding proposals for action of the Climate Resilience Dialogue?
Does the Alliance intend to propose an EU-wide insurance pool for natural disasters?
How does the Commission intend to ensure that any solution at EU level complements national systems, remains budget-neutral and includes incentives for risk prevention?
